posts.title: Mastering Pediatrics: Rash
posts.description: Advancing Learners Pediatric Clinical Reasoning and Knowledge Key Points Rash is a skin eruption or one that causes a change in the appearance, color or texture of the skin. As the skin is the largest organ it can have a lot of changes. Like many problems the differential diagnosis is extremely broad and history and physical examination are very important. Vocabulary is important for describing the skin characteristics. It is more accurate, and communicates the information more consistently. A review of primary skin vocabulary and various colors can be found here . Even experienced non-dermatology clinicians can have problems describing and diagnosing rashes as rashes often seem to have characteristics of more than one type of rash category. You will hear people say things like “it looks virally (meaning more macular) but also has some papules” or “it has a contact distribution from his clothes but he also has it on this other body location.” People will sometimes add the suffix “-oid”

posts.title: Mastering Pediatrics: Ear Pain or Otalgia
posts.description: Advancing Learners Pediatric Clinical Reasoning and Knowledge Key Points Ear pain or otalgia for many people is synonymous with possible acute suppurative otitis media (AOM). Other common causes include middle ear effusion, barotitis, acute otitis externa, or throat, dental or headache pain. For a more novice learner or clinician, performing and describing the ear examination can be difficult because of cerumen, technique and lack of experience and specific vocabulary. The external canal points towards the nose so it is helpful for the examiner to position their body posterior to the ear and aim the tipped otoscope toward the nose within the exernal canal. Repositioning the tipped otoscope may allow cerumen to move out of the field of view or inserting it a couple millimeters more into the external canal may also help. posts.title: Mastering Pediatrics: Abdominal Pain
posts.description: Advancing Learners Pediatric Clinical Reasoning and Knowledge Key Points Abdominal pain has a huge differential diagnosis which changes based on age, gender, and acuity among other variables. It also can encompass referred pain from the back, thorax and pelvic/genitourinary structures, or be a complaint for a general systemic illness. Acute gastroenteritis or constipation are two of the most common reasons for abdominal pain. History can be helpful with crafting a differential diagnosis and evaluation/treatment plan.
